WalkthroughText: When you write `new ClassName(...)`, Java does two things: it allocates a brand-new object on the heap with its own space for each field, and it calls the constructor to initialize those fields. The variable you assign it to (like `Dog myDog`) does NOT hold the object itself — it holds a reference, essentially an arrow pointing to that object's location on the heap. If a variable is instead set to `null`, its arrow points to nothing, meaning there is no object to access. Trying to use a field or method through a null reference causes a NullPointerException, because Java has no object to follow the arrow to.

Choices: A new Dog object is allocated on the heap, its constructor runs setting name to "Rex" and age to 3, and myDog stores a reference to that object
The variable myDog directly stores the text "Rex" and the number 3 inside the stack frame
A new Dog object is created but myDog remains null until a separate assignment statement links them
The Dog constructor creates two separate objects, one for name and one for age
PracticeItems.Explanation: The 'new' keyword allocates a Dog object on the heap and invokes the constructor to initialize its fields; the reference to that heap object is then stored in the variable myDog. It's incorrect to say myDog holds the raw values, since object variables in Java hold references, not the data itself. There's also no separate linking step needed—the assignment happens as part of the single statement.

Choices: d1 points to nothing (no heap object), while d2 holds a reference to a Dog object on the heap with name "Milo" and age 5
Both d1 and d2 point to the same Dog object, since null is a placeholder for the next object created
d1 causes a compile-time error because variables cannot be set to null
d2 is null until the constructor finishes running, then automatically becomes a valid reference to Milo
PracticeItems.Explanation: Setting d1 = null means d1 does not reference any object at all — the arrow from d1 simply points to nothing. d2, however, is assigned a genuine heap object created by 'new Dog(...)', so it holds a valid reference. It's a common misconception that null acts as a 'placeholder' for whatever object is created next, but null and d2's object are entirely unrelated.

Choices: It throws a NullPointerException at runtime because d3 does not reference any object whose field can be accessed
It prints the word "null" to the console
It automatically creates a new Dog object with default field values and prints its name
It causes a compile-time error because d3 was never given a value
PracticeItems.Explanation: Since d3 stores no reference to any heap object (it's null), trying to access d3.name attempts to follow a reference that doesn't exist, causing a NullPointerException at runtime. This compiles fine, since null is a legal value for an object reference, so there's no compile-time error, and Java never auto-creates an object to bail you out of a null reference.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Let's start with a Dog class that has a constructor setting name and age. We begin with an empty stack frame for main.
We declare a variable named d1 of type Dog, but haven't assigned it a value yet — it's uninitialized.
We set d1 equal to null. This means d1 exists as a variable, but its arrow points to nothing — there is no heap object.
Now we declare a second variable, d2, also of type Dog, and prepare to run 'new Dog("Milo", 5)'.
The 'new' keyword allocates a brand-new Dog object on the heap. It starts with default field values before the constructor runs.
The constructor now runs, using the arguments "Milo" and 5 to set the object's fields.
Finally, the reference to this new Dog object is stored in d2 — now d2's arrow points directly at the heap object we just built.
Notice the contrast: d1's arrow points to nothing (null), while d2's arrow points to a real Dog object on the heap with name "Milo" and age 5.
If we tried to access d1.name right now, Java would have no object to follow — this throws a NullPointerException, since d1's arrow leads nowhere.
